tur67-2: According to a Cochrane review of 22 randomised trials and 2,503 people, exercise programmes starting 4–6 weeks after surgery reduced pain and improved daily function slightly faster in the short term than no treatment. Intensive programmes were slightly more effective than mild ones; there was no difference between supervised and home programmes. In no study did exercise increase the rate of re-operation. The quality of the evidence ranged from low to very low.
tur67-3: For avulsion fractures of the bony bump at the base of the bone (not Jones fractures), the boot or rigid-soled shoe is given only for comfort; it does not speed up healing. Wear it when walking, and you can take it off when resting and at night. Wearing a supportive shoe on your uninjured foot protects your other joints. In a multicentre randomised study of avulsion fractures of the base of the bone, pain at 6 months in those treated with a hard-soled shoe was no different from those treated with a cast (in both groups a splint was used for the first week, after which people could put weight on the foot as far as pain allowed), and return to previous activities was earlier (an average of 37 versus 43 days).
tur67-4: A straight neck means that, on a side-view X-ray, the neck vertebrae – which normally sit in a gentle forward curve (lordosis) – look straightened. It is a common diagnosis in Turkey and often causes worry. Yet research shows that straightening is seen about as often in people with neck pain as in people without it. Treating the pain focuses less on the curve on the X-ray and more on how the neck is used.

tur67-6: Another study, by chiropractic researchers, found neck pain more often in people whose curve was 20 degrees or less. This study shows only an association at one point in time; it does not prove that straightening causes pain.
